title: History, Institutions, and Economic Performance: The Legacy of Colonial Land Tenure Systems in India
research_question: Do historical differences in property rights institutions governing land—specifically, whether rights were granted to landlord intermediaries or directly to cultivators—have persistent long-run effects on agricultural investment, productivity, and human development outcomes? If so, through what channels (wealth distribution, political environment, or relations with the state) do these historical arrangements continue to shape contemporary economic performance?
data_description: The analysis uses district-level data on 166 districts across 13 major Indian states that were under direct British rule. Agricultural investment and productivity data (proportion of irrigated area, fertilizer use per hectare, share of area under high-yielding varieties of rice/wheat/other cereals, and crop yields for 15 major crops including rice and wheat) come from the World Bank's India Agriculture and Climate Data Set covering 1956–1987. Health and education infrastructure data (schools, primary health centers) come from the 1981 Census, with literacy rates from 1961–1991 and infant mortality from 1991. Historical measures of non-landlord control are constructed from settlement reports of the 1870s–1880s. Geographic controls include latitude, altitude, rainfall, soil type, and coastal status. Limited colonial-era yield data are available for ten Tamil Nadu districts and 17 Uttar Pradesh districts.
institutional_context: During roughly two centuries of British rule in India, colonial administrators established three broad systems for collecting land revenue: a landlord-based system (zamindari/malguzari), where intermediary landlords held proprietary and revenue-collection rights; an individual cultivator-based system (raiyatwari), where peasants held direct titles; and a village-based system (mahalwari), where village bodies were jointly liable. The choice across districts was shaped by historical accidents including the date of British conquest, the ideologies of individual administrators (e.g., Thomas Munro, Holt Mackenzie), shifts in British economic doctrine, political events such as the 1857 Mutiny (which led to landlord restoration in Oudh), and pre-existing local elites. After independence in 1947, these formal systems were abolished, land reforms were enacted at the state level, and there are no direct taxes on agricultural income, yet the historical institutional variation across districts remained fixed.
